attempts.label: DANDI:000034
attempts.paper_title: SpikeInterface, a unified framework for spike sorting
attempts.entry_title: SpikeInterface spike sorter comparison (Buccino et al. 2020)
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Buccino, Hurwitz, Garcia, Magland, Siegle, Hurwitz and Hennig (2020) on dandiset 000034, which holds the mouse, simulated, rat and retina recordings the paper sorts and two manual curations of its Kilosort2 output. It checks that the recordings are as described, that the curated and ground-truth spike times share the recordings' clocks, and compares the two curations. The findings about sorter outputs are blocked, as three of the six sorters need MATLAB and a GPU, which the runner lacks.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Buccino et al. (2020) from dandiset 000034

outcomes.statement: The dandiset holds the recordings the paper analyses and the files its notebooks name, with the properties the paper and the notebooks give.
outcomes.source: Results, opening paragraph; Data availability; the four notebooks at ee08fb6
outcomes.quote: The datasets are publicly available in NWB format on the DANDI archive
outcomes.notes: All 15 checks hold. The five files the claims file names are present. The mouse 412804 recording is sub-mouse412804_ecephys.nwb, 27,000,000 frames at 30 kHz (900 s), 248 channels (the notebook's count; the paper says 246 active channels). The simulation lasts 600.00 s at 32 kHz and holds 250 ground-truth units. The rat recording has 384 channels at 30 kHz (270.01 s) and the retina recording 1024 channels at 23199.09 Hz (135.73 s). The curated and ground-truth spike times share the clocks of their recordings on the first seconds read (deepest mean trough at lag 0 in median; within 3 frames for 0.88 and 0.86 of the curated units and 0.63 of the ground-truth units).
deviations: The paper's notebook loads a local file, mouse412804_probeC_15min.nwb; the dandiset's mouse recording is matched to it by subject and properties, not by name.

outcomes.statement: The two experts' manual curations of the Kilosort2 output agree on most curated units (226 of 351, 64.2%), and 174 Kilosort2 units are discarded by both.
outcomes.source: Results, Consensus units highly overlap with manually curated ones, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: most of the curated units (226 out of 351–64.2%) are agreed upon by both experts. Notably, 174 units found by Kilosort2 are discarded by both experts
outcomes.notes: Computed from the two curated files under the criterion's second reading (compare_two_sorters of spikecomparison 0.2.6, defaults). Curated 1 has 258 units and curated 2 has 319; 226 are matched and 351 belong to either, 64.39%, so 226 and 351 equal the paper's and 64.39% is within 6.42 of its 64.2%. With a minimum score from 0.3 to 0.8 the matched count goes from 231 to 209, inside its tolerance; the ratio stays inside its tolerance up to 0.7 (59.83%) and falls below it at 0.8 (56.79%, lower bound 57.78%). The criterion fixes the default score of 0.5, so this does not decide the outcome. The count of 174 Kilosort2 units discarded by both curators needs the paper's Kilosort2 run (fig1b-unit-counts, blocked); the curated files hold unit ids and spike times only, with no link to the Kilosort2 clusters (HDF5 tree printed), so it is untested. The criterion gives reproduced when all four values hold under one reading and partially reproduced when 226, 351 and 64.2% hold and 174 does not; with 174 untested the claim is partially reproduced at least, and reproduced only if a Kilosort2 run confirmed the 174. The first reading (compare_multiple_sorters with the Kilosort2 run) could not be run. measured is not given, as the fourth expected value has no measurement.
deviations: spikecomparison 0.2.6 and spikeextractors 0.8.4 were run on NumPy 2 with the removed aliases np.float, np.int, np.Inf, np.product and np.in1d restored as the builtins and functions they stood for.
The curated files carry no sampling rate; their spike times were turned into frames at the mouse recording's 30 kHz, as the paper's loader (NwbSortingExtractor) does with the rate it is given.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds no output of the six spike sorters the paper compares, including the Kilosort2 run that the two experts curated. Every comparison of sorters in the paper, and the comparison of the curations with Kilosort2, can be repeated only by running the sorters again, three of them in MATLAB, and a new Kilosort2 run will not give the units the curators worked on.

The two curated files hold a Units table of ids and spike times only (description 'Autogenerated by NWBFile'), with no sampling rate, no unit labels, no curator name and no link to the Kilosort2 clusters they were curated from; which file is curator 1 and which curator 2 is not stated (the files differ only by session time, 15:55:42 and 15:55:43). Their spike times fall on whole frames at 30 kHz and match the mouse recording's clock.

The retina recording is stored as unsigned 16-bit values centred near 2048 and reaching 4096, consistent with raw counts of a 12-bit converter, while the file states a conversion of 1e-6 V per unit and no offset, which would put every channel near +2 mV. The converter's gain and offset are not in the file.

The mouse 412804 recording stores int16 values with a conversion of 1e-6 V and no gain or channel_conversion per channel. Read that way its band-passed noise SD is about 50 uV and the median curated trough about 455 uV, several times usual Neuropixels levels; at the Neuropixels 1.0 gain of about 0.195 uV per bit the noise would be about 10 uV. The values are consistent with raw counts given a conversion that treats them as microvolts; the file holds nothing to show which.

The electrode tables give location 'unknown' and filtering 'none' for every channel and placeholder group descriptions; the mouse recording has 248 channels where the paper says 246 are active, without marking which; the simulated file does not say which ground-truth cells are excitatory or inhibitory or what noise was added; the archive's species summary lists only house mouse though one recording is from a rat (its file gives 'rattus rattus').

Every raw series is stored in chunks of one channel by 7911 to 26368 frames, so reading a stretch of all channels through h5py fetches one chunk per channel. Streamed from the archive at 0.087 to 0.155 s per chunk in this run, reading a whole recording that way would take 6.2 to 16.9 h; one bulk ranged read of a file ran at 72 MB/s, 1.4 to 6.5 min per recording. These times vary between runs.
The paper gives 226 of 351 curated units as 64.2%; 226/351 is 64.39%.

entries.name: 000034-buccino-2020
entries.title: SpikeInterface spike sorter comparison (Buccino et al. 2020)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Buccino, Hurwitz, Garcia, Magland, Siegle, Hurwitz and Hennig (2020) on dandiset 000034, which holds the mouse, simulated, rat and retina recordings the paper sorts and two manual curations of its Kilosort2 output. It checks that the recordings are as described, that the curated and ground-truth spike times share the recordings' clocks, and compares the two curations. The findings about sorter outputs are blocked, as three of the six sorters need MATLAB and a GPU, which the runner lacks.
